full_judgment:
2. The petitioner's case in short is that the plaintiff-opposite-parties instituted Title Suit No. 288 of 1976 in the 2nd Court of Munsif, Dhaka which was subsequently transferred to the Assistant judge, Savar, Dhaka and re-numbered as Title Suit No. 372 of 1984 for a declaration of title in the suit properties wherein the defendant petitioner was added subsequently. The further case of the petitioner is that the plaintiff instituted the suit alleging that 4.48 acres of land of plot No. 148 of Touzi No. 8173 of mouza Salia under Police Station Savar, District Dhaka originally belonged to the Dhaka Nowab Estate out of which 3.79 acres of land was given in settlement by the Manager of the said Estate under his memo. No. 591 DG 15-8-51 to one Abdur Rashid Bepari son of Abdul Jabbar Fakir of Miton and on receipt of Salami granted receipt on 6-3-58. Said Abdur Rashid Bepari possessed and enjoyed the said land and paid rent to the Nowab Estate upto 1361 BS and during the settlement operation the land was recorded in the name of said Abdur Rashid Bepari at PRR stage. But it was omitted in the copy prepared under section 46 of Estate Acquisition and Tenancy Act and as such objection raised in case No. 73 of 1964 and subsequently the land was recorded in the name of Abdur Rashid Bepari by opening khatian No. 38 who duly paid rent and got DCR. It is also the case, of the plaintiff that the name of said Abdur Rashid Bepari was recorded in the present RS khatian. Thereafter Abdur Rashid Bepari sold the suit properties to different persons including plaintiff Nos. 1 and 2. Plaintiff No. 2 transferred 76 decimals of land to the plaintiff No. 3 out of his purchased 95 decimals and plaintiff No. 4 purchased 1.89 decimals of land from other transferee of Abdur Rashid Bepari. Thereafter when the plaintiffs applied for mutation of their names in the RS khatian they found the name of Saidur Rahman already mutated in the khatian. The plaintiffs then filed Misc. Case No. 34 of 1975 before the defendant No. 1 who found that the Circle Officer (Rev) was not the competent authority to record the name of predecessor of Abdur Rashid Bepari and mutation of Saidur Rahman's name was also found illegal and order passed for cancellation of the name of Abdur Rashid Bepari and treated the suit properties as government khas land and that compelled the plaintiffs to file the present suit for declaration that the orders of the defendant No. 1 dated 6-8-1987 are illegal, null and void and the plaintiffs are the lawful owners of the suit property. 

 7. Mr. Shamsul Huq Choudhury, the learned Advocate appearing for the plaintiff-opposite parties, submits that the Trial Court has not committed any illegality in allowing the amendment by order dated 15-11-1989 as amendment may be made at any stage of the proceedings even upto appellate stage and the present amendment has not in any way changed the character and nature of the suit as well as of the plaint. Relying on a decision reported in 29 DLR (SC) 311 (Golam Hafiz Mia Vs. Khadem Ali Meah) the learned Advocate submits that amendment of the pleading can be made at any stage of the suit provided such amendment does not prejudice the interest of the other party which it has got by lapse of time nor it would change the nature of suit. He argued that during the pendency of the suit the plaintiffs were dispossessed from the suit land for which previously an amendment petition was filed praying for inserting a prayer for recovery of khas possession of the suit land and the present amendment was found necessary for specifying the boundary of the suit land. This amendment has not in any way changed the character and nature of the suit as well as of the plaint. 

 8. The learned Advocate for the opposite party relying on another decision reported in 28 DLR 131 (Sultan Ahmed Vs. Purna Chandra Karmaker and others) submits that amendment of the plaint can be allowed when it does not alter the averment of the plaint. According to the learned Advocate, the amendment which is in question now has not altered the averment of the plaint which remained as it was and only for getting an effective decree in the suit the schedule of the plaint has been amended by incorporation of certain boundaries which has not altered the averment made in the plaint in any manner whatsoever. Relying on another decision reported in 12 DLR 626 (Daguram Mandal Vs. Omela Shundari Bewa) the learned Advocate for the opposite parties submits that the amendment made in the plaint has not changed the character and nature of the suit and of the plaint but the amendment indicated a full and correct description of the properties in suit which is necessary for passing an effective decree. This amendment provided a right and correct description of the land in suit. The learned Advocate submits that after previous amendment the suit became a suit for declaration of title and recovery of khas possession and the last amendment is nothing but incorporation of correct description of the suit land and it has not prejudiced the defendants in any way and it only removed the mis-description of the property for getting an effective decree. 

 9. From the perusal of the papers filed it appears that the plaintiff filed the suit praying for a declaration that the plaintiffs are the rightful owners of the schedule property and that the orders passed by the defendant No. 1 on 6-8-76 is null and void and that the name of the plaintiff should be recorded in the present RS khatian in respect of the schedule of land showing 0.95 decimals of land in favour of the plaintiff No. 1, 0.18 in favour of plaintiff No. 2, 0.76 in favour of plaintiff No. 3 and 1.90 in favour of plaintiff No. 4 after releasing it from the khas khatian of the government. The plaintiff at the time of filing the plaint described the suit property as follows : 

 10. The plaintiffs then filed a petition for amendment of the plaint by adding words "out of 14.15 acres of land" in the schedule after the words 0.79 decimals of land. Admittedly the plaintiffs subsequently filed another amendment petition wherein they prayed for recovery of khas possession of the suit land. These amendments were not challenged before any higher Court by any of the defendants. The plaintiff opposite parties again filed another petition for amendment of the plaint and in that petition the plaintiffs prayed for inserting specific boundary in the schedule, as according to them there will be difficulty in getting a decree for khas possession if the land is not specifically described. 

 12. Now the question is whether this amendment has changed the character of the plaint. The learned Advocate for the plaintiff opposite parties has not controverted the principle of law set-forth in the decision reported in 13 DLR 871 that by way of amendment the character of the plaint cannot be changed but he submitted that amendment has not changed the character of the plaint and he further argued that as the suit ultimately turned into a suit for recovery of khas possession such an amendment became necessary for getting an effective decree. 

 14. At the time of filing the suit their case was that they were in possession of the suit land. But subsequently they came with the plea that during the pendency of the suit they have been dispossessed from the suit land and at their instance the prayer portion was amended by adding recovery of khas possession. When such an amendment is made the plaintiffs at the same-time ought to have prayed for amendment of the schedule of the land so that it may clearly indicate for which land they want recovery of khas possession. Subsequently the plaintiff filed a petition giving specific boundary from where they wanted to eject the defendants or, to say, recover their possession. In the case reported in 12 DLR page 626 the fact was that the application was for pre-emption by a co-sharer of the property transferred by kabala and what happened was that by some unfortunate error the property was described with reference to the Charcha Survey and not with reference to the CS Khatian. The court found that the Trial Court rightly allowed the amendment and decided the real question in dispute between the parties. The principle of law enunciated in that decision is that amendment may be allowed for giving specific description of the land for which the suit has been filed. In the present suit before us amendment was made describing clearly the land for which the plaintiff prayed for recovery of khas possession. In the case reported in 28 DLR 130 it has been held that where an amendment of the plaint in a suit does not alter the averment of the plaint but is sought in view of the subsequent happenings after the filing of the suit, such prayer for amendment can be allowed. Here in the present suit after filing of the suit the plaintiff made a prayer for recovery of possession alleging that during the pendency of the suit they have been dispossessed from the suit land. But while amending the plaint they failed to properly describe the land for which they prayed for recovery of khas possession. The present amendment in question has not changed the character and nature of the suit as the plaint has been amended making the present suit a suit for recovery of possession and also for declaration. 

 15. The learned Advocate for the petitioner while pressing the petition relied on the decision reported in 13 DLR 871 wherein it has been held that an amendment which if allowed would change the character of the plaint though not the character of the suit cannot be allowed as that will prejudice the defendant in his defence. In the said suit the plaintiffs case as stated in the plaint originally was that he had paid to defendant and the latter had received certain amount of money. When it was proved that the defendant could not and did not receive the money from the plaintiff, the latter wanted to say that somebody else on behalf of the defendant received the money and wanted to amend the plaint to that effect; but it was held that could not be done as it would change the character of the plaint. The present suit as it stands now after all previous amendments is a suit for declaration with prayer for recovery of khas possession. But in the present amendment certain specific boundary has only been incorporated in keeping the other averments intact. This amendment, therefore, has not changed the character of the plaint. It is therefore found that the facts leading to the case reported in 13 DLR 871 and facts and circumstances of the present case before us are different. In that view of the matter I hold that the case reported in 13 DLR 871 has no manner of application in the facts and circumstances of the present case before us. The latest amendment has practically removed the mis-description in the schedule which has not in any way prejudiced the defendant petitioner. Further also it appears that after allowing the amendment the Trial Court has already allowed the defendant to file additional written statement if they so desire. Thus after considering the materials on record and after hearing the learned Advocates of both the sides I hold that the amendment made by order dated 15.11.1989 has not changed the character of the plaint and the Trial Court has not committed any illegality which may call for any interference by this court at this stage.
